source.title: Spectral Norm Regularization for Improving the Generalizability of Deep Learning

record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization-gap differences across regularization methods and batch sizes, and measures properties correlated with the gap; it does not test the claim's random-label memorization premise.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own measurements of test accuracy/generalization gap under four training methods and two batch sizes, plus input-gradient norms and Hessian eigenvalues compared with the gap. Cited results about large batches and sharp minima are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study compares held-out accuracy at batch sizes 64 and 4096 under four regularization recipes. DenseNet on CIFAR-100 has matched 200-epoch budgets and directly tests V5. Other settings use longer large-batch training. Input gradients, unscaled Hessian eigenvalues, and singular-value spectra do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: spectral norm regularization improves generalizability in their experiments, and test-input sensitivity tracks the gap better than the examined training-input gradients or maximum Hessian eigenvalues. Their superiority statements need qualification: spectral does not have the best small-batch accuracy in every setting or the smallest threshold-defined gap in every table entry.
record.recipe_differences: Uses spectral norm regularization, vanilla SGD, weight decay, and adversarial training on image classifiers; measures accuracy, generalization gaps, input-gradient norms, Hessian eigenvalues, and singular spectra. Does not use random-label memorization, width sweeps, or magnitude-aware sharpness tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports variation by batch size (64 versus 4096), dataset, model, and training method. STL-10 used cropping and horizontal flip augmentation.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-input loss-gradient norms correlate positively with the gap, whereas training-input norms have negative correlations for DenseNet/CIFAR-100, VGGNet, and NIN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input sensitivity measured on test examples correlates with generalization gaps across these training trajectories; training-input sensitivity need not track them in the same direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Regularized DenseNet models can have larger maximum Hessian eigenvalues despite better generalization; spectral regularization has the largest eigenvalues.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled maximum Hessian eigenvalues do not consistently rank generalization across different regularization recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: Spectral norm regularization produces a flatter singular-value spectrum in the selected weight matrix than the tested alternatives.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectral norm regularization changes weight-matrix singular-value spectra differently from weight decay and adversarial training.

record.problems: Only four image-classification settings are tested. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The generalization-gap comparison uses setting-specific test-accuracy thresholds, and several property measurements are shown in figures without full numeric values. The study does not test random labels, width, architecture comparisons, adaptive optimizers, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removing memorized examples.
record.rows_left_out: none noted; all tabled results for each of the four methods, two batch sizes, and four model-dataset settings are included. Figure-only property measurements are included where they bear on the tested gap-property version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected models and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning-dependent comparisons.

Language models, batch-size thresholds, warmup, normalization changes, and controlled effects of longer training. Fixed-epoch comparisons are available only for DenseNet on CIFAR-100. Large-batch initial learning rates are already increased tenfold.
Dropout and its interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbations, matched low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 1 numbers match the supplied text. States for paired batch comparisons concern held-out accuracy, not regularization-versus-vanilla improvements. Threshold-defined gaps use different alpha values across batch sizes and should not substitute for the batch accuracy comparison. VGGNet, NIN, and STL-10 still show lower large-batch accuracy with longer training, but those results do not isolate V5's fixed-epoch premise. No V7 verdict is warranted, and STL-10's regularization comparisons do not justify the record's V5 limits_scope label.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Language models, workload-dependent batch threshold, epoch-budget comparisons, and recipe changes involving learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization.
Dropout effects and interaction with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.

rows.subject: DenseNet
rows.operation_detail: Computed maximum Hessian eigenvalue of training and test loss using power iteration and compared with generalization gap.

conditions.value: vanilla, weight decay, adversarial training, spectral norm regularization

rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: Figure 3 only; precise values not stated. Text reports regularized models tend to have larger eigenvalues and spectral has largest despite best generalizability.
rows.note: The authors conclude this measure is not suggestive for predicting generalizability.
rows.check: An unscaled maximum Hessian eigenvalue is not V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure. Its contrary ordering cannot challenge that version.

rows.note: This describes weight spectra; it is not the magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness measure in V7.
rows.check: Weight-matrix singular-value spectra do not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with generalization gaps.
